title: Chest Pain Triage: STEMI, Serial Troponin, Unstable Angina and Procedure-Related MI
summary: Learn why ST elevation goes to reperfusion without waiting for troponin, why one early normal troponin cannot rule out infarction, how unstable angina is defined in the high-sensitivity era, and how the 2026 definition changed procedure-related MI.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 19 Hit 2 (STEMI → reperfusion without waiting for biomarkers), Hit 5 (type 4a / type 5 MI), Hit 6 (unstable angina), Trap 1 (normal troponin, sent home) and the type 4a and type 5 rows of the Number Vault. Checked against the Fifth Universal Definition of MI (Mills 2026), Domienik-Karłowicz 2021 (Fourth UDMI and ESC guideline summary) and Paiva 2024. Hit 5 and the Number Vault give the 2018 multiples (4a > 5×, type 5 > 10× within 48 h); the 2026 definition no longer relies on biomarker thresholds and uses a 30-day window, so the lesson teaches both and marks the multiples as historical (register flag rv-procedural-mi-thresholds). Hit 6 says unstable angina is “managed like NSTEMI”; the sources describe a more favourable prognosis, no practical guideline algorithm after MI is excluded and likely less benefit from routine early revascularization, so that phrase is not taught (register flag rv-ua-management-context). Not taught: the reinfarction > 20% rule over 3–6 h (the 2026 text says rising serial values suggest recurrence; pending), the hs-cTn ng/L rows, door-to-ECG 10 min, and natriuretic-peptide, hs-CRP, D-dimer and homocysteine rows.

objectives: Explain why ST elevation on the ECG leads to reperfusion without waiting for troponin.
Explain why a single early troponin below the 99th percentile cannot rule out MI and describe serial testing pathways.
Define unstable angina and contrast the 2018 and 2026 criteria for procedure-related MI.

scenes.title: Three chest-pain patients
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients in the emergency department. (1) Chest pain with new ST-segment elevation in two contiguous ECG leads; troponin still pending. (2) Rest chest pain that began 1 hour ago, non-diagnostic ECG, first high-sensitivity troponin below the 99th percentile. (3) A patient 6 hours after a coronary stent procedure whose troponin has risen to about 7 times the 99th percentile. Question token: “Wait, repeat, or prove?”

cues.text: Three chest-pain patients. The first has new ST-segment elevation on the ECG, and the troponin result is still pending.
The second has had rest pain for one hour, a non-diagnostic ECG, and a first high-sensitivity troponin below the 99th percentile.
The third is six hours after a coronary stent, with troponin about seven times the 99th percentile. Wait, repeat, or prove?

scenes.title: The ECG comes first
scenes.altText: Schematic ECG strip with ST-segment elevation. Card “Working diagnosis of STEMI” (Fifth Universal Definition, 2026): new ST elevation at the J-point in at least two contiguous leads — ≥1 mm in most leads, with higher sex- and age-specific thresholds in V2–V3 — without left ventricular hypertrophy or left bundle branch block. Card “Do not wait for troponin”: the 12-lead ECG rapidly identifies acute coronary occlusion needing immediate reperfusion; troponin can still be below the 99th percentile in about 1 in 6 patients with ST elevation in the first hours. Token: the final STEMI diagnosis still needs acute myocardial injury on troponin.

cues.text: In chest pain, the 12-lead ECG comes first. It is the fastest way to find a blocked coronary artery that needs immediate reperfusion.
A working diagnosis of STEMI needs new ST-segment elevation in at least two neighbouring leads: one millimetre in most leads, more in leads V2 and V3.
Troponin cannot be relied on in the first hours. In about one in six patients with ST elevation, it is still below the 99th percentile.
So reperfusion does not wait for the lab. Troponin later confirms the final diagnosis by showing acute myocardial injury.

props.title: Working diagnosis: STEMI
lines: New J-point ST ↑ in ≥ 2 contiguous leads
≥ 1 mm most leads; more in V2–V3

scenes.title: No ST elevation: serial troponin
scenes.altText: Schematic troponin-versus-time curve: detectable rise 2–3 h after symptom onset, peak at 12–24 h, elevated for days to weeks. Card “One early value can miss MI”: sensitivity of the 99th percentile at presentation is about 90% overall and as low as 70% within 3 h of symptom onset. Card “Serial pathways”: 0/1 h or 0/2 h high-sensitivity algorithms with assay-specific thresholds and deltas (preferred in the ESC guidance summarised by Domienik-Karłowicz 2021); an extra sample at 3 h if inconclusive and still suspicious; conventional pathways use a risk score with the 99th percentile at 0 and 3 h. Token: early presenters need serial testing.

cues.text: Without ST elevation, troponin takes over, but timing matters. Troponin starts to rise about two to three hours after symptoms begin, peaks at twelve to twenty-four hours, and stays up for days.
So one early value can miss an infarct. The 99th percentile catches about ninety percent of infarcts at presentation, but as few as seventy percent within three hours of onset.

High-sensitivity pathways repeat the test at one or two hours, using thresholds and changes specific to each assay. If the result is unclear and suspicion remains, another sample is taken at three hours.
The rule: in a patient who presents early, a normal first troponin does not rule out infarction. Serial testing is needed.

props.title: One early value can miss MI
Serial pathways
lines: Extra sample at 3 h if unclear

scenes.title: Unstable angina and procedure-related MI
scenes.altText: Card “Unstable angina”: new ischaemic symptoms at rest or minimal exertion, or a sudden worsening of chronic angina, with myocardial infarction excluded by serial troponin; more likely with ischaemic ECG changes; part of the ACS spectrum (NSTE-ACS = NSTEMI + unstable angina, differing by troponin release); rarer with high-sensitivity assays, with a more favourable prognosis than MI. Card “After a procedure”: Fourth UDMI (2018) type 4a after PCI = cTn >5× the 99th percentile within 48 h plus ischaemia, imaging or angiographic evidence; type 5 after CABG = >10×. Fifth UDMI (2026): procedure-related MI within 30 days needs acute myocardial injury plus clinical/ECG features and is confirmed by an angiographic complication or new imaging loss of viable myocardium; it does not rely on fixed biomarker thresholds (higher, still-rising values, e.g. >5× URL at 6 h after intervention or >35× at 24 h after surgery, make it likely). Hook answers card.

cues.text: Unstable angina is new ischaemic chest pain at rest or with minimal effort, or suddenly worsening angina, when serial troponins exclude infarction. Ischaemic ECG changes make it more likely. It is still acute coronary syndrome, but rarer with high-sensitivity assays, and with a better outlook than infarction.

After a procedure, the 2018 definition used multiples: type 4a after a stent needed troponin over five times the 99th percentile within forty-eight hours, and type 5 after bypass surgery over ten times, each with supporting evidence. The 2026 definition drops fixed thresholds: within thirty days, a troponin rise with clinical or ECG features is confirmed by an angiographic complication or new loss of viable muscle on imaging.
Hook answers. Patient one goes straight to reperfusion. Patient two needs a repeat troponin. Patient three needs confirmation on angiography or imaging, not just a multiple.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 2 Early, normal cTn: repeat at 1–2 h
3 After stent: confirm on angio or imaging

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Chest pain, normal troponin → send home” (✓ an early troponin can be normal; serial testing and the ECG decide); “ST elevation: wait for the troponin” (✓ STEMI is a working diagnosis from the ECG; reperfusion does not wait); “No troponin rise = no ACS” (✓ unstable angina is ACS with serial troponins below the 99th percentile).

cues.text: Trap one: chest pain with a normal troponin, so send the patient home. No: an early troponin can be normal. Serial testing and the ECG decide.
Trap two: ST elevation, so wait for the troponin. No: the ECG makes the working diagnosis and reperfusion does not wait.
Trap three: no troponin rise means no acute coronary syndrome. No: unstable angina is acute coronary syndrome with normal serial troponins.

props.title: ✗ “Normal troponin → send home.”
lines: ✓ Early cTn can be normal; repeat it

scenes.title: Look, repeat, prove
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “LOOK, REPEAT, PROVE.” LOOK at the ECG first (ST elevation → reperfusion now); REPEAT the troponin when the ECG is quiet (one early value is not a rule-out; ischaemia with normal serial values = unstable angina); PROVE the complication after a procedure (the 2026 definition needs angiographic or imaging confirmation, not a fixed multiple). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: look, repeat, prove. Look at the ECG first. Repeat the troponin when the ECG is quiet. Prove the complication after a procedure.

Where it breaks: the ECG can miss an occluded artery, up to one in four patients managed as NSTEMI; some pathways rule out on a single very low value with assay-specific thresholds; and unstable angina is only confirmed when angiography shows an acute coronary lesion.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: ECG misses some occlusions (≤ 1 in 4 NSTEMI)

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “ST elevation → reperfuse now · quiet ECG → serial troponin”, “Ischaemia + normal serial troponin = unstable angina · after a procedure, prove the complication”.

cues.text: Read the ECG first and reperfuse ST elevation without waiting for troponin, repeat troponin when the ECG is quiet because an early value can be normal, call ischaemia with normal serial troponins unstable angina, and confirm a procedure-related infarction with angiography or imaging rather than a troponin multiple.

props.label: ST elevation → reperfuse now · quiet ECG → serial troponin
Ischaemia + normal serial cTn = UA · after a procedure, prove it

explanation.what: Plain language: in chest pain, the heart tracing is read first because a blocked artery can show on it before the blood test rises. When the tracing is quiet, the blood test is repeated, because an early result can still be normal. Chest pain from a threatened heart with normal repeated troponins is unstable angina. After a heart procedure, a high troponin alone is not enough: a complication has to be shown. Scientific terms: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), J-point, contiguous leads, reperfusion, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn), 99th percentile upper reference limit (URL), 0/1 h and 0/2 h algorithms, non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS), unstable angina, procedure-related MI, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
explanation.why: Troponin is released from dying muscle over hours: it rises about 2–3 h after onset and peaks at 12–24 h, so it can be normal when the patient arrives, even with an occluded artery. Procedures themselves release troponin, so a number alone cannot separate expected procedural injury from infarction.
explanation.measure: STEMI working diagnosis: new J-point ST elevation in ≥ 2 contiguous leads (≥ 1 mm in most leads; higher in V2–V3). About 1 in 6 STEMI patients have troponin below the 99th percentile in the first hours. Sensitivity of the 99th percentile at presentation ≈ 90%, ≈ 70% within 3 h of onset. Serial hs-cTn at 0/1 h or 0/2 h with assay-specific thresholds and deltas; extra sample at 3 h if inconclusive. 2018: type 4a > 5× and type 5 > 10× the 99th percentile within 48 h with supporting evidence. 2026: procedure-related MI within 30 days, troponin rise plus clinical or ECG features, confirmed by an angiographic complication or imaging; both are required when the complication arose during the procedure or the procedure was done for acute MI.
explanation.differs: STEMI (ECG decides, troponin confirms later) vs NSTEMI (troponin rise and/or fall) vs unstable angina (ischaemia with normal serial troponins); 2018 numbered types with multiples vs 2026 procedure-related MI without fixed thresholds.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next step for ST elevation with troponin pending, the next step after one early normal troponin, naming unstable angina from ischaemic pain with normal serial troponins, or recognising that procedural MI needs more than a troponin multiple.

right.label: NSTEMI / unstable angina
points: NSTEMI: rise/fall above 99th pct; UA: serial cTn normal

comparisons.distinguisher: ECG first; then serial troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina.

comparisons.title: Procedure-related MI: 2018 vs 2026

right.label: Fifth UDMI (2026)
points: Confirmed by complication on angiography or imaging

comparisons.distinguisher: A biomarker multiple versus proof of a procedural complication.

mnemonic.text: LOOK, REPEAT, PROVE: look at the ECG first, repeat the troponin when the ECG is quiet, prove the complication after a procedure.
mnemonic.explanation: Orders the three decisions: ECG for occlusion, serial troponin for NSTEMI versus unstable angina, confirmation for procedure-related MI.
mnemonic.limitation: The ECG misses some occluded arteries (up to 1 in 4 patients managed as NSTEMI); some pathways rule out MI on one very low value with assay-specific thresholds; unstable angina is confirmed only when coronary angiography shows atherothrombosis or another acute coronary pathology.

analogyLimitations: ECG and troponin curve are schematic.
Thresholds and serial-sampling intervals are assay-specific and follow local pathways.
takeaway: Read the ECG first and reperfuse ST elevation without waiting for troponin, repeat troponin when the ECG is quiet because an early value can be normal, call ischaemia with normal serial troponins unstable angina, and confirm a procedure-related infarction with angiography or imaging rather than a troponin multiple.

questions.stem: A patient with ongoing chest pain has new ST-segment elevation of 2 mm in two contiguous inferior leads. The first troponin is not yet reported. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Proceed on the reperfusion pathway without waiting for troponin
options.rationale: Correct. The ECG gives the working diagnosis of STEMI and identifies occlusion needing immediate reperfusion; troponin may still be below the 99th percentile early.

options.text: Wait for the troponin; treat only if above the 99th percentile
options.rationale: Incorrect. Troponin can be below the 99th percentile in the first hours in about 1 in 6 STEMI patients.

options.text: Repeat troponin at 3 hours before deciding
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serial troponin pathways are for patients without ST elevation.

options.text: Order CK-MB to confirm infarction first
options.rationale: Incorrect. The ECG already identifies an occlusion needing immediate reperfusion, and troponin, not CK-MB, is the preferred biomarker because CK-MB has lower sensitivity and specificity.

questions.stem: A patient has rest chest pain with transient ST depression. High-sensitivity troponin at 0, 1 and 3 hours is below the 99th percentile each time, with no significant change. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Ischaemic symptoms with ECG changes and MI excluded by serial troponins fit unstable angina, part of the ACS spectrum.
Incorrect. NSTEMI needs a rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile.
Incorrect. Chronic injury needs troponin above the 99th percentile that is stable; here all values are normal.

options.text: No ACS; normal troponin rules it out
options.rationale: Incorrect. Normal serial troponins exclude infarction, not unstable angina.

questions.stem: Several hours after an uncomplicated elective coronary stent, a patient develops new chest pain with ischaemic ECG changes, and troponin is rising. Under the Fifth Universal Definition of MI (2026), which finding confirms procedure-related MI?

options.text: Stent thrombosis in the treated vessel on repeat angiography
options.rationale: Correct. After an initially uncomplicated procedure, procedure-related MI within 30 days is confirmed by a coronary complication such as stent thrombosis, or by a new regional wall motion abnormality or loss of viable myocardium on imaging.

options.text: Troponin above 5 times the 99th percentile alone
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 2026 definition does not rely on biomarker thresholds; higher, rising values make it likely but do not confirm it.

options.text: Any troponin above the 99th percentile within 48 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. Procedures commonly raise troponin; a value above the 99th percentile shows injury, not infarction.

options.text: Chest discomfort the morning after the procedure
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many patients have some chest discomfort after procedures; symptoms alone do not confirm infarction.

references.citation: Mills NL, Newby LK, Zaman S, et al. Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026). Glob Heart. 2026;21(1):64. doi:10.5334/gh.1578
references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. ECG as cornerstone for identifying acute coronary occlusion needing immediate reperfusion; STEMI ECG criteria; troponin below the 99th percentile URL early in about 1 in 6 STEMI patients; final STEMI diagnosis needs acute injury; troponin kinetics (rise 2–3 h, peak 12–24 h); sensitivity ~90% overall, ~70% within 3 h; 0/1 h, 0/2 h and 0/3 h pathways; early presenters need serial testing; single-sample rule-out pathways; up to 1 in 4 NSTEMI with acute occlusion; unstable angina definition, prognosis and ACS status; comparison table of Fourth UDMI type 4a/5 criteria; Box 5 procedure-related MI criteria (30 days, no fixed biomarker threshold, example >5× URL at 6 h after intervention and >35× at 24 h after surgery); chest discomfort common after procedures; recurrent MI (rising serial values suggest recurrence; CK-MB adds cost without clarity); biomarkers other than troponin not used routinely; acute injury = rise/fall with ≥ 1 value above the 99th percentile URL, chronic = stable elevation.

references.citation: Domienik-Karłowicz J, Kupczyńska K, Michalski B, et al. Fourth universal definition of myocardial infarction. Selected messages from the European Society of Cardiology document and lessons learned from the new guidelines on ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and non-ST-segment elevation-acute coronary syndrome. Cardiol J. 2021;28(2):195-201. doi:10.5603/cj.a2021.0036
references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. Fourth UDMI periprocedural (≤ 48 h) type 4a (5×) and type 5 (10×) thresholds with normal baseline; > 20% rise if baseline elevated; ESC NSTE-ACS 0 h/1 h then 0 h/2 h algorithms with assay-specific cut-offs and deltas, extra 3-h sample if inconclusive, 0 h/3 h still recommended at a lower level.

references.citation: Paiva L, Vieira MJ, Baptista R, Ferreira MJ, Gonçalves L. Unstable Angina: Risk Stratification for Significant Coronary Artery Disease in The Era of High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin. Glob Heart. 2024;19(1):7. doi:10.5334/gh.1286
references.usedFor: Europe PMC full text. NSTE-ACS comprises NSTEMI and unstable angina, differing in biomarker release; patients formerly called unstable angina reclassified as NSTEMI with hs-troponin; guidelines lack a practical algorithm for unstable angina after MI is excluded; likely less benefit from routine early revascularization than MI.

claims.text: ECG identifies acute occlusion needing immediate reperfusion; STEMI working-diagnosis criteria; troponin below the 99th percentile early in about 1 in 6 STEMI; final diagnosis needs acute injury.
Troponin kinetics; sensitivity at presentation ~90% and ~70% within 3 h; early presenters need serial testing; 0/1 h, 0/2 h, extra 3-h sample, 0/3 h pathways.
Unstable angina definition; ischaemic ECG makes it more likely; confirmed on angiography; part of ACS (NSTE-ACS); rarer with hs-troponin; more favourable prognosis.
Fourth UDMI: type 4a > 5× and type 5 > 10× the 99th percentile within 48 h with supporting evidence.

Fifth UDMI: procedure-related MI within 30 days, no fixed biomarker threshold, confirmed by angiographic complication or imaging (both when the complication arose during the procedure or in acute MI); chest discomfort common after procedures.
Up to 1 in 4 patients managed as NSTEMI have acute occlusion; single-sample rule-out pathways with assay-specific thresholds.
Reviewer items not taught: unstable angina “managed like NSTEMI”; reinfarction > 20% rise over 3–6 h; door-to-ECG 10 min; hs-cTn ng/L thresholds.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 19 Hit 5 and the Number Vault give the Fourth UDMI multiples (type 4a > 5×, type 5 > 10× within 48 h; reinfarction > 20%). The Fifth UDMI (Mills 2026) defines procedure-related MI within 30 days without fixed biomarker thresholds, confirmed by an angiographic complication or imaging (register flag rv-procedural-mi-thresholds).

Ch. 19 Hit 6 says unstable angina is “managed like NSTEMI”. Mills 2026 notes a more favourable prognosis; Paiva 2024 notes guidelines give no practical algorithm after MI is excluded and that benefit from routine early revascularization is likely smaller than in MI. The lesson teaches unstable angina as ACS without the management claim (register flag rv-ua-management-context).
